quote: Chris Hibbert compared my view to Bartley’s Pan-Critical Rationalism
content: The comparison is apt and worth more than the sentence gives it. Bartley's The Retreat to Commitment (1962 — a book, no DOI) argued exactly this: that a rationalist need not exempt anything, including the rational stance itself, from criticism, and that the appearance of a regress comes from confusing justification with criticizability. It also drew a well-known formal objection — that a position defined as "comprehensively criticizable" runs into self-reference problems of the liar's family, argued by Post and pressed by Watkins in exchanges through the 1970s and '80s — which is precisely the difficulty this essay ends by admitting it has not formalized. Reading Bartley and his critics would supply both the position and the sharpest available statement of its unsolved problem, rather than leaving it as an open personal project.

quote: treating transistors inside the AI just as if they were transistors found in the environment, not an ad-hoc special case
content: This prediction — that a correctly built reflective agent "shouldn't have to do anything special" — is the one claim here that has since been tested by serious formal work, and it did not hold. Naturalizing the agent into the environment is what the later literature calls embedded agency, and it breaks the standard framework at several points at once: expected utility theory presupposes a clean agent-environment boundary, self-referential trust in one's own future reasoning runs into the Löbian obstacle that Yudkowsky and Herreshoff's tiling-agents work identified, and reasoning about one's own computations requires a theory of logical uncertainty that did not exist until logical induction (Garrabrant et al., 2016) and remains impractical. Garrabrant and Demski's "Embedded Agency" (2018) is a catalogue of what goes wrong. The naturalistic intuition may still be correct; "it shouldn't require anything special" is the part that has been falsified.

quote: we’ve concluded that differential equations (which few humans master) are actually simpler (in an information-theoretic sense) than heroic mythology
content: The information-theoretic sense of "simpler" is not available for this comparison in the way the sentence assumes. Kolmogorov complexity is defined only relative to a universal machine and only up to an additive constant, and the invariance theorem that makes it well-behaved asymptotically says nothing about which of two particular finite descriptions is shorter — a point made forcefully about Solomonoff induction by Sterkenburg (British Journal for the Philosophy of Science, 2016). Writing down Maxwell's equations also requires specifying the real numbers, vector calculus, and a field ontology, none of which is free; "Thor" is short only because the reader already has an enormous agent-model to point at, which is exactly the objection being made against Thor. The honest version of the claim is that physics is simpler relative to a formal language chosen after the fact by physicists, which is a weaker and more interesting statement.

quote: One of the ways I license using induction and Occam’s Razor to consider “induction” and “Occam’s Razor” is by appealing to E. T. Jaynes’s principle
content: Jaynes's maxim is a rule about conditioning: within a probability calculation, do not throw away evidence, and do not use different information at different points, on pain of the inconsistencies he spent his career cleaning up. It is a constraint on the application of a fixed inference rule, not a licence to use that rule to validate itself. Reading "use all the information available" as "therefore use induction when evaluating induction" equivocates between evidence and inference rules, which is a distinction Jaynes was careful about. The underlying position may be defensible — Van Cleve and Alston defend it — but not on this authority.

quote: But I haven’t yet sat down and formalized the exact difference—my reflective theory is something I’m trying to work out, not something I have in hand.
content: The admission is fair, and the gap it names is the whole load-bearing distinction of both essays. It is also not an untouched problem: epistemologists have been trying to say when epistemic circularity is benign for forty years, and the sharpest formulation of why the reflective loop is hard to license is the easy-knowledge problem — that a rule which vindicates itself also vindicates any rule whatever, including crystal-ball gazing, when applied by its own lights. "Meta-level loops feel different from object-level circles, and common sense can tell them apart" is not a criterion; it is the observation that we like our own loop. Two decades on, no formal separation has been produced from this direction, which is at least weak evidence that the informal one was doing less work than it appeared to.
